raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old male patient presented to the outpatient department with a history of mid-back pain for 1 year and progressive weakness in both lower limbs for 3 months. The pain in the mid-back was insidious in onset, progressive in nature, dull-aching in character, initially aggravated by walking and movements of the trunk but had pain even at rest at the time of presentation. Back pain was also associated with a history of difficulty in walking and pain in both lower limbs for the past 3 months. The patient walked with help of walking aid. There was no history of trauma or constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight and loss or loss of appetite. He consulted elsewhere, where he was clinicoradiologically diagnosed with spinal tuberculosis and was started on the anti-tubercular therapy, but there was no relief in his symptoms even after 2 months of taking anti-tubercular therapy. The family and personal history were not significant. On examination, there was deep tenderness over the thoracolumbar junction. There was no local warmth/swelling over the back. The neurological examination suggested paraparesis [Table 1].
Thoracolumbar radiographs (AP/Lateral) and CT scan suggested huge lytic lesions with complete destruction of T12 and L1 vertebral body as well as pedicles and posterior elements and complete collapse of body of T12 with partial collapse of the body of L1 [Figure 1]. MRI suggested abnormal marrow signal intensity lesion involving vertebral body and posterior elements with pathological collapse of T12 with similar signal intensity changes in T11 and L1 bodies [Figure 1]. Prominent flow voids were seen in predominantly anterior but also posterior epidural space from T9-L2, likely to be prominent epidural blood vessels [Figure 1]. The primary differential diagnoses were spinal tuberculosis and neoplastic etiologies. After discussion with the patient and his family, the patient was advised surgical decompression. After informed consent, the patient was operated under general anesthesia wherein T9 to L3 stabilization with pedicle screw instrumentation and anterior decompression by pediculectomy of the left T12 and L1 by a posterior approach was performed. The surgeon encountered massive bleeding at the time of anterior decompression and was controlled by the use of local and systemic hemostatic agents. A vascular etiology of spinal compression was suspected and tissue from the destroyed vertebrae was sent for histopathological examination and culture-sensitivity tests. The histopathological examination suggested no evidence of malignant cells/granuloma. Culture sensitivity testing and TB-PCR were negative for infection. DSA was performed after 2 months of surgery through the right femoral artery which revealed EDAVFs fed by the vessels arising from T10-L2 vertebrae and transcatheter embolization of the predominant right T12 feeders was performed with 25% glue (2 ml) [Figure 2]. Angiographically, it was an extradural Type 1 single vessel dural fistula. However, the atypical nature of massive vertebral destruction precluded it from grouping into any single entity. DSA performed after the embolization revealed 30 % reduction of fistula fed by vessels from the right T12 pedicle [Figure 2]. At follow-up after 21 months of surgery, the patient is free from pain, walking independently with normal neurological examination findings [Figure 3].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old male presented with a 1-year history of mid-back pain and a 3-month history of progressive lower extremity weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with insidious, progressive, dull-aching mid-back pain over 1 year, initially aggravated by walking and trunk motion but now present at rest. Over the last 3 months, back pain was accompanied by bilateral lower extremity pain, difficulty walking, and reliance on walking aids. He denied history of trauma, fever, chills, anorexia, or weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Empirically treated for presumptive spinal tuberculosis with antitubercular therapy for two months without clinical response. No personal or family history of note.
subjective.review_of_systems: Complained of mid-back pain, bilateral lower extremity pain, weakness, and ambulation difficulty. Denied fever, weight loss, or anorexia. Home medications: prior empiric antitubercular therapy. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Deep tenderness over the thoracolumbar junction without local warmth or superficial swelling. Neurological examination revealed spastic paraparesis with difficulty walking.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracolumbar radiographs and CT: large lytic destructive lesions with complete destruction of T12 and L1 vertebral bodies, pedicles, and posterior elements, complete collapse of T12, and partial collapse of L1. Thoracolumbar MRI: abnormal marrow signal involving T12 with pathological collapse, similar marrow changes in T11 and L1, and prominent epidural flow voids from T9 to L2 (consistent with engorged epidural blood vessels). Spinal surgery: T9-L3 posterior pedicle screw stabilization and anterior decompression via left T12-L1 pediculectomy, complicated by profuse intraoperative epidural hemorrhage. Histopathology of vertebral tissue: no granulomas and no malignant cells. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA): demonstrated an extradural arteriovenous fistula (EDAVF, Type 1 single vessel dural fistula) fed by vessels from T10-L2.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Extradural arteriovenous fistula (EDAVF, Type 1 single vessel dural fistula) of the thoracolumbar spine causing massive vertebral destruction (T12-L1) and compressive myelopathy, mimicking spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease) and spinal neoplasm. Intraoperative tissue biopsy demonstrated absence of granulomas or malignant cells, and bacterial cultures and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR (TB-PCR) were negative, ruling out spinal tuberculosis.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed with urgent surgical decompression (left T12 and L1 pediculectomy) and T9-L3 posterior pedicle screw instrumentation, followed by digital subtraction angiography (DSA) and successful endovascular transcatheter embolization of feeding vessels at T12 with 25% n-butyl cyanoacrylate glue. Antitubercular therapy was discontinued. At 21-month follow-up, the patient was completely pain-free, ambulating independently without aids, with normal neurological examination.
